chapters.n: Amos was not a professional prophet but a herdsman from Tekoa, a village south of Bethlehem in Judah. He was sent north to preach to Israel around 760 BC, a time of prosperity under King Jeroboam II.

f.g: A village about 10 miles (16 km) south of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness.

chapters.n: Amos’s theme sentence: the Lord roars like a lion from Jerusalem. Even the green pastures and fertile Mount Carmel wither at His voice. Amos, a shepherd, knew what a lion’s roar meant.

f.w: The LORD will roar from Zion

f.g: A lush, wooded ridge on Israel’s northern coast; if Carmel dries up, everything does.

chapters.n: Amos begins with Israel’s enemies. “Three transgressions, and for four” is a Hebrew way of saying “sin upon sin, more than enough.” Damascus (Syria) brutally crushed the Israelite region of Gilead.

f.g: A numeric pattern (x, x+1) meaning the sins have piled up past the limit.

chapters.n: Fire will consume the royal houses of Syria. Hazael and Ben-hadad were Syrian kings who had attacked Israel.

f.g: A name or title used by several kings of Damascus.

chapters.n: The gates of Damascus will be broken and its people exiled to Kir. This came true when Assyria conquered Damascus in 732 BC.

f.g: The heavy beam that locked the city gate.
“Valley of wickedness” — probably a wordplay on a place name.

chapters.n: Gaza, a Philistine city, captured whole communities and sold them as slaves to Edom. Trafficking in human beings is condemned.

f.g: A Philistine city on the southern coast.
Entire populations, not just soldiers.

chapters.n: The same fire of judgment will burn Gaza’s walls and palaces.

f.g: A refrain repeated for each nation, stressing that God’s justice is consistent.

chapters.n: The other Philistine cities — Ashdod, Ashkelon, and Ekron — will also fall. God’s judgment reaches the whole Philistine league.

f.g: In KJV, “GOD” in capitals represents the divine name YHWH (Jehovah).

chapters.n: Tyre also sold captives to Edom, breaking a “brotherly covenant” — perhaps the old treaty of friendship between Hiram of Tyre and David and Solomon.

f.g: Tyre, the great Phoenician port city.

chapters.n: Tyre’s strong island walls will not save it from God’s fire.
Edom, descended from Esau, kept attacking Israel, his “brother” Jacob’s descendants, with relentless hatred. Unforgiving anger is a sin God judges.

f.g: Literally “destroyed his compassions” — smothered all natural family feeling.

chapters.n: Teman and Bozrah, Edom’s major cities, will burn.

f.g: A region or city in Edom, known for its wise men.

chapters.n: The Ammonites committed horrific war crimes against pregnant women just to grab more land. Amos insists God holds even foreign nations accountable for cruelty.

f.g: A people east of the Jordan, descended from Lot.
Expand their territory.

chapters.n: Rabbah, Ammon’s capital (modern Amman, Jordan), will be destroyed amid battle cries and storm.

f.g: A violent storm — a picture of God’s overwhelming power.

chapters.n: Ammon’s king and his officials will be carried away together into exile.

f.g: Hebrew malkam; some see a wordplay on Milcom, Ammon’s god.

chapters.n: Moab desecrated the corpse of Edom’s king, burning his bones to powder. Notice that this crime was not against Israel — God cares about justice among all peoples.

f.g: A nation east of the Dead Sea, descended from Lot.

chapters.n: Fire will consume Kerioth, a Moabite city, and Moab will fall in the noise of battle.
Moab’s ruler and leaders will be killed. The judge (the chief official) stands for the government as a whole.

f.g: The ruler or chief magistrate.

chapters.n: Now Amos turns closer to home — to Judah, his own nation. Their sin is rejecting the Lord’s law and following the lies, or false gods, their ancestors served.

f.w: despised the law of the LORD

f.g: Probably false gods or idols, which deceive their worshipers.

chapters.n: Jerusalem’s palaces will burn too. This was fulfilled when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587/586 BC.
The climax: Israel itself. Listeners who enjoyed hearing their enemies condemned now hear their own sins named. They sold innocent and poor people into slavery for money or the price of sandals.

f.g: Sandals — a trifling debt, or the token used to transfer property.

chapters.n: The rich trample the poor into the dirt and push the humble aside. Father and son use the same young woman, dishonoring God’s name.

f.w: pant after the dust of the earth on the head of the poor
f.g: Eagerly crush the poor into the dust.

f.w: turn aside the way of the meek

chapters.n: They lounge at their altars on garments taken as loan security — which the law said must be returned by night — and drink wine bought with unfair fines.

f.g: Wine paid for with fines extracted from people.

chapters.n: God reminds Israel what He did for them: He destroyed the giant-like Amorites, root and branch, so Israel could live in the land.
He brought them out of Egypt and guided them forty years in the wilderness. Their ingratitude makes their sins worse.

f.w: I brought you up from the land of Egypt

chapters.n: God gave them prophets and Nazarites — living examples of devotion. “Isn’t that so?” He asks.
But Israel tempted the Nazarites to break their vows and silenced the prophets. Rejecting God’s messengers is rejecting God.
God says He is weighed down by Israel like an overloaded cart. Some translate it as God pressing them down instead; either way, the weight of sin is crushing.

f.g: The Hebrew is uncertain; it may mean “I will crush you as a loaded cart crushes.”

chapters.n: When judgment comes, no one escapes — not the fast runner or the strong man.

f.w: the flight shall perish from the swift

chapters.n: Archers, sprinters, and cavalry — all of Israel’s military strength will fail.

f.w: he stand that handleth the bow
f.g: The archer — he will not hold his ground.

chapters.n: Even the bravest soldier will throw off his gear and flee. Human strength cannot stand against God.

f.g: Without armor or outer clothing — stripped of everything.

chapters.n: The Lord addresses all twelve tribes — the whole family He rescued from Egypt. The message is for northern Israel and southern Judah alike.

f.g: All the descendants of Jacob.

chapters.n: Being chosen carries responsibility. God “knew” Israel in a close covenant relationship, so He holds them more accountable, not less.

f.g: “Known” means chosen, loved in covenant.

chapters.n: A series of questions shows cause and effect. Two people walking together have agreed to meet; likewise, a prophet speaks because God has met with him.

f.w: Can two walk together, except they be agreed?
f.g: “Agreed” can mean “have made an appointment.”

chapters.n: A lion roars only when it has caught prey. Amos implies that when God “roars” through a prophet, judgment is real.

f.g: A strong young lion, hunting on its own.

chapters.n: A bird is not caught without a trap, and a trap doesn’t spring for nothing. Every effect has a cause — including Israel’s coming troubles.

f.g: A trap or snare.

chapters.n: A trumpet in the city makes people afraid. When disaster comes, the Lord is behind it. Amos teaches that God governs history.

f.g: Here “disaster” or “calamity,” not moral evil.

chapters.n: A key verse for Latter-day Saints: God does nothing without first revealing His plans to His prophets. He warns before He acts.

f.w: he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets

f.g: Hebrew sod — the private counsel of God.

chapters.n: Just as everyone fears when a lion roars, a prophet cannot keep quiet when God speaks. Amos explains why he must preach.
Ironically, Philistines and Egyptians are invited to look at Samaria’s chaos and oppression. Even pagans would be shocked.

f.g: A Philistine city.
Capital of the northern kingdom of Israel.

chapters.n: Israel’s rich no longer know how to do right; their mansions are full of goods taken by violence.

f.g: Their treasure houses are stocked with stolen wealth.

chapters.n: An enemy will surround the land and plunder the palaces. Assyria conquered Samaria in 722 BC.
A shepherd might rescue only scraps — two legs or an ear — to prove a sheep was killed by a lion. So only scraps of Israel’s luxury-loving elite will survive.

f.w: two legs, or a piece of an ear

f.g: The Hebrew is unclear; possibly “on the damask cushion of a couch.”

chapters.n: The Lord calls witnesses to testify against Israel (“the house of Jacob”).

f.g: God of armies — Lord over all heavenly and earthly powers.

chapters.n: Judgment will strike Bethel, where Jeroboam I set up a golden calf. The horns on the altar corners, a place of refuge, will be broken off.
The wealthy’s winter and summer homes and their ivory-paneled mansions will be destroyed. Archaeologists have found carved ivory pieces in Samaria.
Amos bluntly calls the wealthy women of Samaria “cows of Bashan” — well-fed and pampered. They demand drinks from their husbands while their luxury is funded by crushing the poor.

f.g: Kine = cows. Bashan, east of the Sea of Galilee, was famous for rich pasture and fat cattle.
Husbands (literally “lords”).

chapters.n: God swears by His own holiness that they will be dragged away with hooks. Assyrian carvings show captives led by ropes attached to hooks.

f.g: The Hebrew may mean hooks or harpoons; the picture is of being hauled off helplessly.

chapters.n: They will be led out single file through holes broken in the city wall, each one straight ahead, and thrown out toward Harmon (the meaning of that place is uncertain).

f.g: Gaps knocked in the city wall by attackers.
Hebrew obscure; often read “cast out toward Harmon,” perhaps a place name.

chapters.n: With heavy sarcasm Amos mimics a priest: “Come to Bethel and sin! Go to Gilgal and sin even more!” Their busy religion at false shrines only adds to their guilt.

f.g: Or “every three days” — mocking their over-eager, showy devotion.

chapters.n: They love to show off their offerings and announce their generosity. Their worship is about themselves, not God or their neighbors.

f.g: Yeast; normally excluded from offerings burned on the altar (Leviticus 2:11).
This is what you love.

chapters.n: Now God lists warnings He already sent. First, famine — “clean teeth” because there was nothing to eat. Yet they did not come back to Him. This refrain repeats five times.

f.g: An ironic phrase for hunger: no food to dirty their teeth.

f.w: yet have ye not returned unto me

chapters.n: God held back the rain just before harvest, when it was needed most, and let it fall in one town but not another, so they could see His hand in it.
Thirsty people staggered from town to town looking for water but found too little. Still they did not return to God.

f.g: Staggered, reeled from weakness.

chapters.n: Crop diseases and locusts destroyed their gardens, vineyards, figs, and olives. Still they did not return.

f.g: A kind of locust.

chapters.n: Plague like the plagues of Egypt, and war that killed young men and left the stench of the dead in their camps. Still they did not return.
Some places were devastated like Sodom and Gomorrah; Israel was like a burning stick yanked from the fire. Even that close call did not turn them back.

f.w: a firebrand plucked out of the burning

chapters.n: Because every warning failed, a final encounter is coming: “Prepare to meet thy God.” In context a warning, these words also invite all of us to be ready to stand before God.
Amos describes the God they must meet: Creator of mountains and wind, who knows human thoughts and controls day and night. A hymn-like verse that magnifies His power.

f.w: declareth unto man what is his thought
f.g: Or reveals His own thoughts to man — through prophets (Amos 3:7).

f.w: The God of hosts, is his name

chapters.n: Amos sings a funeral song over Israel, even while the nation is still alive and prosperous. Announcing a funeral for the living was a shocking way to warn them.

f.g: A funeral dirge, sung in a distinctive limping rhythm in Hebrew.

chapters.n: Israel is pictured as a young woman who has fallen and has no one to lift her up.

f.g: A poetic personification of the nation.

chapters.n: War will cut Israel’s armies down to a tenth. A town that sent a thousand soldiers will see only a hundred return.
The heart of Amos’s message: seek the Lord and live. Life comes from a relationship with God, not from rituals.

f.w: Seek ye me, and ye shall live

chapters.n: Don’t look for God at the popular shrines of Bethel, Gilgal, and Beersheba. There are wordplays: Gilgal will go into exile (galoh yigleh) and Bethel will become nothing.

f.g: A town far south in Judah; northerners made pilgrimages there.
Bethel (“house of God”) will become Beth-aven (“house of nothing”), as Hosea 4:15 puns.

chapters.n: Seek the Lord and live — or His judgment will spread through Israel like fire that Bethel’s gods can’t put out.

f.g: The northern kingdom, led by Joseph’s descendants Ephraim and Manasseh.

chapters.n: Those who make justice bitter and cast righteousness to the ground are addressed. Justice that should heal has become poison.

f.g: A very bitter plant; a symbol of bitterness and sorrow.
Justice, fair rulings.

chapters.n: Seek the Creator who placed the star clusters, turns deep darkness into dawn, and pours the sea’s waters on the land. The same God who controls nature will judge.

f.g: The Pleiades cluster and the constellation Orion.
Deepest darkness.

f.w: calleth for the waters of the sea

chapters.n: God can suddenly empower the weak and plundered against the strong, so that even fortresses fall.

f.g: Destruction, ruin (or those who have been plundered).

chapters.n: The powerful hate anyone who stands up for justice at the city gate, where court cases were heard.

f.g: The city gate was the public courthouse and marketplace.

chapters.n: Because they tax the poor heavily, their fine stone houses and vineyards will not benefit them. They will lose what they gained unfairly.

f.g: Heavy grain levies or rents.

f.w: ye shall not dwell in them

chapters.n: God sees their many sins: persecuting the innocent, taking bribes, and denying the poor their rights in court.
In such a corrupt time, wise people keep quiet — or perhaps they will be stunned into silence when disaster comes.

f.g: The wise or shrewd.

chapters.n: Seek what is good, not evil, and live. Then the Lord really will be with you, as you already claim He is.

f.g: Israel boasted that God was on their side; Amos says that is true only if they seek good.

chapters.n: Hate evil, love good, and make the courts fair. Perhaps the Lord will be gracious to what remains of Israel. Amos offers hope, but no guarantee.

f.w: Hate the evil, and love the good

chapters.n: Because they won’t repent, mourning will fill the streets. Even farmers will be called to wail alongside professional mourners.

f.g: Professional mourners hired for funerals.

chapters.n: Even the vineyards — normally places of joyful harvest songs — will hear wailing, because the Lord will pass through in judgment, as He once passed through Egypt.
Israel looked forward to “the day of the Lord” as a day of victory. Amos warns: for the wicked, it will be darkness, not light.
A vivid picture: escaping a lion only to meet a bear, then reaching home and leaning on the wall — and a snake bites you. There is no escape.

f.g: An image of danger striking where one feels safest.

chapters.n: Amos repeats for emphasis: the day of the Lord will be pitch dark, without a glimmer of light, for those unprepared.
Strong words: God hates their religious festivals. Worship without justice and mercy disgusts Him.

f.g: God will not accept the aroma of their sacrifices.

f.w: I hate, I despise your feast days

chapters.n: Burnt offerings, grain offerings, and fattened peace offerings — God will accept none of them, since they come from unrepentant hearts.

f.g: Grain offerings.

chapters.n: Stop the noisy hymns and harp music! Beautiful worship music means nothing to God when hearts are unjust.

f.g: Harps or lyres; stringed instruments.

chapters.n: Amos’s most famous line: let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream. God wants justice that never dries up. Martin Luther King Jr. quoted it in the civil rights movement.

f.w: let judgment run down as waters

f.g: An ever-flowing stream — unlike wadis that dry up in summer.

chapters.n: God asks: during the forty years in the wilderness, did you really offer Me sacrifices from the heart? The question suggests their worship was compromised even then.
They carried idols of foreign star gods along with them. Stephen quoted this verse in his defense before the Sanhedrin.

f.g: Probably Sakkuth, an Assyrian god; the Greek translation reads “Moloch.”
Probably Kaiwan, an Assyrian name for the planet Saturn, worshiped as a god.

chapters.n: Therefore Israel will go into exile beyond Damascus — that is, to Assyria. This happened in 722 BC.
Woe to the comfortable elites of Jerusalem and Samaria who feel secure and important. Complacency is a spiritual danger — a warning repeated in the Book of Mormon for our day.

f.g: Mockingly, “the first of the nations” — they thought of themselves as top-tier.

chapters.n: Look at other cities like Calneh, Hamath, and Gath. Are you better than they? Those cities had fallen or would fall — so could you.

f.g: A city in northern Syria.
A major Syrian city on the Orontes River.
A Philistine city.

chapters.n: They push thoughts of disaster far away, yet their violent ways bring it closer.

f.g: The day of disaster or judgment.

chapters.n: They lounge on ivory-inlaid beds, eating choice lambs and fattened calves. This was luxury most Israelites could never afford.

f.g: Sprawl lazily.

chapters.n: They make up idle songs to the harp, imagining themselves as musical as King David — but without his devotion.

f.g: Improvise or strum idly.

chapters.n: They drink wine by the bowlful and use the finest perfumes, but they don’t grieve at all over the coming ruin of their nation.

f.g: The ruin of Israel (the house of Joseph).

chapters.n: So those who were “first” in luxury will be first into exile, and their partying will end.

f.g: Hebrew marzeaḥ — a feasting club or revelry.

chapters.n: God swears by Himself that He despises Israel’s pride and fortresses, and He will hand the city over to its enemies.

f.g: The pride of Israel — their arrogant confidence.

chapters.n: Even if ten men survive in a house, they will die. The destruction will be thorough.

f.g: A small remnant; even that remnant won’t survive.

chapters.n: A grim scene: a relative comes to carry out bodies for burial. A survivor is told, “Hush! Don’t mention the Lord’s name” — afraid of drawing more judgment.

f.g: Possibly one who burns spices for the dead, or who burns bodies during a plague.
Hebrew has — “Hush!” — a word that sounds like our “shh.”

chapters.n: At the Lord’s command, both large and small houses will be shattered. No social class is exempt.

f.g: Breaks, cracks — perhaps from earthquake.

chapters.n: Do horses gallop on cliffs? Does anyone plow rock with oxen? Of course not — yet Israel has done something just as absurd by turning justice into poison.

f.g: A poisonous, bitter plant.
Bitter wormwood; something deadly.

chapters.n: They boast about capturing Lo-debar and Karnaim by their own power. Amos puns: Lo-debar means “nothing,” and Karnaim means “horns” (strength).

f.g: Hebrew lo dabar — also the name of a town Israel captured.
Hebrew Qarnayim — another captured town; horns symbolize strength.

chapters.n: God will raise up a nation — Assyria — to oppress Israel from its northern border to its southern edge, the very territory Jeroboam II had won.

f.g: Probably a valley stream near the Dead Sea, Israel’s southern limit.

chapters.n: The first of five visions: God forms a swarm of locusts just as the second crop begins to sprout, after the king had taken his share. Losing this crop would mean starvation.

f.g: Locusts.
The first cutting of hay, apparently taken as a royal tax.

chapters.n: As the locusts finish eating, Amos pleads, “Lord, forgive! How can Jacob survive? He is so small.” The prophet intercedes for the very people he warns.

f.g: The people of Israel, called by their ancestor’s name.

chapters.n: The Lord relents: “It will not happen.” Prayer matters; a prophet’s plea changed what came next.

f.g: Relented, changed course — not that God had sinned.

chapters.n: Second vision: the Lord calls for a judgment by fire so fierce it dries up the great deep beneath the earth and starts consuming the land.

f.g: Or “the land” — the allotted portion of farmland.

chapters.n: Again Amos begs God to stop, using the same plea: Israel is too small to survive this.

f.g: Stop, hold back.

chapters.n: Again the Lord relents. Twice mercy wins — but the next visions show patience has limits.
Third vision: the Lord stands beside a wall built true to a plumb line, holding a plumb line in His hand.

f.g: A string with a weight, used by builders to check whether a wall is perfectly vertical.

chapters.n: God will measure Israel against His standard. Like a crooked wall, they will be found out of line, and He will no longer overlook it. This time Amos doesn’t intercede.

f.g: Overlook their sins; spare them.

chapters.n: Israel’s shrines will be destroyed, and the royal house of Jeroboam will fall by the sword. Jeroboam II’s son Zechariah was assassinated after only six months.

f.g: Here a poetic name for Israel.

chapters.n: Amaziah, the priest at the royal shrine of Bethel, reports Amos to the king as a traitor. Authorities often call God’s messengers troublemakers.

f.g: Not the same as King Amaziah of Judah.

chapters.n: Amaziah twists Amos’s words slightly; Amos had spoken against Jeroboam’s house, but the message of exile was accurate.

f.w: Jeroboam shall die by the sword
f.g: Amos actually said the sword would come against “the house of Jeroboam” (v. 9).

chapters.n: Amaziah sneers, “Go home to Judah, seer, and make your living prophesying there.” He assumes Amos preaches for pay.

f.g: Earn your living.

chapters.n: “Don’t prophesy at Bethel; this is the king’s sanctuary.” Amaziah treats the shrine as belonging to the king, not to God.

f.g: The royal sanctuary — a state temple.

chapters.n: Amos answers: “I was not a professional prophet or trained in a guild. I was a herdsman and tended sycamore figs.” His authority came from God’s call, not credentials.

f.g: A member of a prophetic school or guild (“sons of the prophets”), as in 2 Kings 2:3.
The sycamore fig had to be nicked to ripen; it was poor man’s fruit.

chapters.n: “The Lord took me from following the flock and said, ‘Go, prophesy to my people Israel.’” Like David, Amos was called from shepherding.

f.w: the LORD took me as I followed the flock

chapters.n: Amos turns the tables on Amaziah: you tell me not to preach against Israel? Then hear what God says about you.

f.g: Don’t let your words drip — don’t preach.

chapters.n: Amaziah’s family will suffer the horrors of conquest, his land will be divided among others, and he himself will die in exile in a pagan land. Israel will surely go into captivity.

f.g: Measured out with a surveyor’s cord and given to new owners.
An unclean, foreign land.

chapters.n: Fourth vision: a basket of ripe summer fruit, gathered at the end of the growing season.

f.g: Hebrew qayitz — late-summer fruit such as figs.

chapters.n: A wordplay: “summer fruit” (qayitz) sounds like “end” (qetz). Israel is ripe — its end has come. God will no longer overlook its sins.

f.g: Hebrew qetz, a pun on qayitz (summer fruit).

f.w: I will not again pass by them

chapters.n: Temple songs will turn into wailing, and dead bodies will be everywhere, thrown out in stunned silence.

f.g: Or “Hush!” — the same word as in Amos 6:10.

chapters.n: Amos again targets those who trample the needy and try to wipe out the poor.

f.g: Trample or devour the poor.

chapters.n: Merchants can’t wait for holy days to end so they can get back to cheating: shrinking the measure, inflating the price, and rigging the scales. Their religion is only outward.

f.w: making the ephah small, and the shekel great
f.g: Using a smaller measure for grain sold and a heavier weight for silver received — cheating both ways.

chapters.n: They buy the poor into slavery for a trifle and sell sweepings of wheat as if it were good grain.

f.g: Chaff and husks swept up from the floor.

chapters.n: God swears He will never forget what they have done. Sin that is not repented of remains on the record.

f.g: Ironically, God swears by Israel’s pride — something as fixed as His own being — or by Himself, “the Pride of Jacob.”

chapters.n: Because of this, the whole land will heave like the Nile in flood, rising and sinking. An earthquake may be in view.

f.g: The Nile, which rose and fell every year.

chapters.n: The sun will set at noon and darkness will fall in broad daylight. A solar eclipse visible in Israel in 763 BC may have given this image force.

f.w: cause the sun to go down at noon

chapters.n: Celebrations will turn to funerals. People will wear sackcloth and shave their heads, mourning as for an only son.

f.g: Shaving the head was a mourning custom.

chapters.n: A sobering prophecy: a famine not of food but of hearing God’s word. Latter-day Saints often see this fulfilled in the Great Apostasy, when prophets and priesthood authority were withdrawn.

f.w: hearing the words of the LORD

chapters.n: People will search everywhere, from sea to sea, but will not find the word of the Lord. Revelation is a gift that can be lost.
Even the strongest, healthiest young people will faint from thirst — spiritual and physical.
Those who swear by the idols of Samaria, Dan, and Beersheba will fall and not rise. False worship cannot save.

f.g: Probably a goddess or the calf idol worshiped there.
Literally “the way to Beersheba” — the pilgrimage route, perhaps meaning its deity.

chapters.n: The fifth and final vision: the Lord stands by the altar and orders the shrine’s pillars struck so the building collapses on the worshipers. No one will escape.

f.g: Probably the altar at Bethel, the center of Israel’s false worship.
The capital or top of a pillar.

chapters.n: There is nowhere to hide from God — not the depths of the earth or the heights of heaven. A dark reversal of Psalm 139’s comfort.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the world of the dead, imagined as deep below.

f.w: though they climb up to heaven

chapters.n: Not the forests on top of Mount Carmel or the bottom of the sea will hide them; God commands even the sea serpent.

f.g: A wooded, cave-filled ridge — a natural hiding place.
A sea monster; God controls even the chaos creatures of the deep.

chapters.n: Even in exile they will not be safe. God will watch them “for evil, and not for good” — the opposite of His usual protective care.

f.w: I will set mine eyes upon them

chapters.n: Another hymn of God’s power: He touches the earth and it melts; the land heaves like the Nile.

f.w: as by the flood of Egypt

chapters.n: He builds His upper rooms in the heavens and sets the sky’s vault over the earth; He pours out the seas. The Lord is His name.

f.g: Upper chambers — God’s heavenly palace.
Vault or dome (of the sky).

chapters.n: A startling question: Are you any different to Me than the Ethiopians? I guided other peoples’ migrations too. Being chosen does not make Israel immune to judgment.

f.g: Cushites, from the far south along the Nile — a distant people.
Probably Crete, the Philistines’ place of origin.

chapters.n: The sinful kingdom will be destroyed — but not completely. A remnant of Jacob’s house will survive. Hope begins to dawn.

f.w: I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob

chapters.n: Israel will be scattered among all nations as grain is shaken in a sieve — yet not a single grain will be lost. God keeps track of every scattered Israelite, the basis for the promised gathering.

f.w: I will sift the house of Israel among all nations
yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth

chapters.n: The sinners who said, “Disaster won’t touch us,” will die. Overconfidence is no protection.

f.g: Old English “come before,” meaning “meet” or “confront.”

chapters.n: Restoration! God will rebuild David’s fallen “booth.” James quoted this at the Jerusalem council, applying it to Gentiles joining the Church through Christ, the Son of David.

f.g: Booth or hut — David’s dynasty, now a fallen shelter.

f.w: In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David

chapters.n: Restored Israel will possess what remains of Edom and of all nations called by the Lord’s name. The Greek version read “that the rest of mankind may seek the Lord,” the form James quoted.

f.w: which are called by my name

chapters.n: Harvests will be so abundant that plowing season overtakes reaping, and grape-treading runs into sowing. Mountains will drip with sweet wine — a picture of millennial plenty.

f.w: the plowman shall overtake the reaper
the mountains shall drop sweet wine

chapters.n: God will bring His people back. They will rebuild ruined cities and actually enjoy their vineyards and gardens — reversing the curses of Amos 5:11.

f.g: Restore the fortunes; bring back the exiles.

chapters.n: The book ends with a promise: God will plant Israel in their land, never to be uprooted again. Judgment is not God’s last word — restoration is.

f.w: I will plant them upon their land
